questions.explanation: Ice core and marine sediment records show the pacing: summer insolation at high northern latitudes rose and fell on orbital timescales, and the terminations line up with insolation maxima. Ice albedo, dust, and greenhouse gases amplified and extended whatever the orbit started, which is why carbon dioxide is read as a feedback on the pacing rather than as the clock itself. questions.explanation: Sinking air is compressed by the weight of the air above it, and compression raises temperature far faster than it can add water vapour, so relative humidity falls. That is the mechanical reason subsiding zones are dry and inversion-prone, and it needs no change in soil moisture to operate. The alternative stories invert the physics: compression does not delete vapour, it does not lift dew points upward, and a pressure gradient is not a moisture gradient.

questions.explanation: Snow is bright, so a fresh covering reflects most of the sunlight that reaches it; bare ground is darker and absorbs the rest. Losing the cover therefore raises absorbed shortwave, which melts more, which removes more cover, and the loop closes on a warming cause. The feedback is self-reinforcing rather than self-limiting, which is the definition that distinguishes it from the dry-air and water-vapour effects. Reading a drier surface as brighter is the classic error here, because dry soil is darker than wet soil, and shading by trees is not what the snow-albedo loop runs on.

questions.explanation: Gas solubility in seawater falls as temperature rises, so warming moves carbon dioxide from the dissolved pool into the atmosphere. answer.exemplar: A deepening active layer exposes previously frozen organic soil to microbial decomposition, which releases carbon dioxide and, in waterlogged conditions, methane. Those gases add greenhouse forcing, which warms the ground further and thaw advances into the next layer of organic material, so the original warming drives more thaw that drives more warming and the loop closes on itself. That self-reinforcing return path is what makes it a feedback rather than a one-way consequence, which would be a thaw that stops once the warming stops. The timescale matters too: the active layer responds within years while the deep permafrost pool warms far more slowly, so the strength should not be read from the borehole depth alone.

questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies that deepening exposes new organic matter, that decomposition of that matter emits greenhouse gases, and that those gases add forcing which thaws still more ground, closing a self-reinforcing loop rather than a one-way change. It should also distinguish the fast active layer from the slow deep permafrost pool so the borehole depth is not over-read. Naming only more thaw, or only more carbon in the soil, describes a component of the loop without the return path that makes it a feedback at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the newly exposed frozen material releases, and where that release leads.

questions.explanation: Cooling and the addition of salt both raise seawater density, so cold salty water sinks and spreads southward at depth while warm surface water flows north to replace it. The northward limb carries heat from the tropics into the North Atlantic, which is why the circulation redistributes rather than creates energy. Calling it the Gulf Stream confuses one surface limb of the whole overturning with the system, and a mode of North Pacific atmospheric variability is a pattern of pressure differences rather than a density-driven heat transport.

answer.exemplar: Sulfate aerosol scatters incoming shortwave radiation back to space, and it also supplies extra cloud condensation nuclei so that clouds contain more, smaller droplets and reflect more sunlight, so regions with heavy emissions are held cooler than they would be under greenhouse forcing alone. Because the aerosol is produced where coal and heavy industry sit, the cooling is concentrated over and downwind of those regions, which leaves land and the clearer air of the Southern Hemisphere warming faster than the ocean and the polluted north. The pattern is consistent with that mechanism but not proof of it, because natural ocean-atmosphere variability can also produce a patchy temperature field, stratospheric aerosol from eruptions adds a short-lived cooling of its own, and cloud responses differ between regions, so several candidates can reproduce a single spatial contrast.

questions.explanation: A strong answer links aerosol shortwave scattering and brighter clouds to uneven cooling, ties the geography to where the aerosol is emitted, and then concedes that the observed pattern is not unique because natural variability and volcanic stratospheric aerosol can mimic it. An answer that treats aerosols only as a uniform global dimmer loses the spatial argument, and one that treats the pattern as proof of aerosol cooling fails to note that several mechanisms can generate the same contrast, which is what keeps such findings out of the settled category.
questions.hint: Separate the physical effect of the aerosol from where it is produced, then ask what else could mimic the pattern.

questions.explanation: Outgoing infrared rises 56 watts per square metre over the 20 kelvin span, which is 2.8 per kelvin, while a black surface at 290 K would rise by 4 sigma T cubed, about 5.5 per kelvin. Because the model loses less energy to space per kelvin than it gains in sunlight, its net feedback is positive. The same 2.8 figure with the opposite verdict is the trap, since a muted loss is not a muted gain: the test compares the infrared response against the absorbed solar increase, not against zero, and the 5.5 value is the blackbody limit rather than the measured slope.
questions.hint: Find the slope of outgoing infrared against surface temperature, then compare it with a black surface.
questions.learningObjective: diagnose the sign of the net feedback from an outgoing infrared versus temperature slope

options.text: About 2.8 W per square metre per kelvin, below a black surface, so the feedback is positive

options.misconception: believes a muted infrared loss damps the response rather than amplifying it
options.text: About 2.8 W per square metre per kelvin, above a black surface, so the feedback is negative

options.misconception: substitutes the blackbody derivative for the slope the model actually produces
options.text: About 5.5 W per square metre per kelvin, which is the bare black surface at 290 K

options.misconception: doubles the temperature span when forming the slope from the table
options.text: About 1.4 W per square metre per kelvin, because the 20 kelvin span is read as 40

questions.explanation: The stratosphere sits above the surface and gains heat mainly by absorbing outgoing infrared there, so it cools when the surface and the troposphere above it warm, which is why the ozone layer and upper stratosphere have cooled while the surface warmed. Tropospheric warming in turn deepens the troposphere and raises its water vapour content, so a whole column of air warms together and the pattern is a fingerprint of where the heating is being taken up. The idea that greenhouse gases warm every layer equally, or that layer thickness sets the response, ignores this vertical structure entirely.
questions.hint: Compare the two layers: one sits directly above the surface and one sits above the tropopause.
questions.learningObjective: explain the vertical pattern of surface warming with stratospheric cooling

options.text: Ozone loss cools the stratosphere while surface warming warms the troposphere below

options.misconception: believes every atmospheric layer warms by the same amount from the same gas
options.text: Greenhouse gases warm every layer of the atmosphere by the same amount at once

options.misconception: believes a layer's mass sets how much it warms from added gas
options.text: The stratosphere warms more slowly because it is thinner and holds less of the gas

options.misconception: believes insolation alone controls the stratosphere's temperature trend
options.text: The stratosphere is colder simply because it receives far less sunlight through the year

questions.explanation: The series steps by about 0.6 K between the two blocks and the only documented change is the move to a traffic junction, which is the classic signature of an inhomogeneity rather than a climate signal, and no nearby station steps at the same year. Homogenisation adjusts the record by comparing against surrounding stations or an overlap period, which is the only method that can tell a site change from a regional one. Smoothing, discarding years, or switching averaging rules each leave the discontinuity in place, and a genuine regional step would show up in the neighbouring stations as well.
questions.hint: Ask whether the neighbouring stations step at the same year as this one does.
questions.learningObjective: identify a station inhomogeneity and choose a homogenisation method

options.text: A step artefact from the 1964 move, fixed by comparing nearby long-record stations

options.misconception: believes a discontinuous record is a real climate signal worth smoothing
options.text: A genuine step in climate, best shown by smoothing the series with a running mean

options.misconception: believes the fault is confined to the four years after the move
options.text: An error in the 1960s alone, fixed by discarding the four years after the move

options.misconception: believes a change in averaging rule explains a persistent step
options.text: A change in the averaging rule, fixed by recomputing with the pre-1964 years only

questions.explanation: An ensemble perturbed only in initial conditions samples how the internal variability of ocean and atmosphere can move a projection, so member density says how common a trajectory is within that sampled set and nothing about how likely the true response is. Turning that density into a probability for a physical outcome is the error, and a member far from the others may be a poor numerical configuration rather than a physical impossibility. Calling the spread an error bar that the truth cannot leave also misreads it, because a wider or narrower set of trajectories changes with the perturbation chosen.
questions.hint: Ask what was perturbed between the members, and therefore what the spread represents.
questions.learningObjective: judge what an ensemble spread can and cannot tell you about probability

options.text: Partly wrong, because the spread samples internal variability, not outcome probability

options.misconception: believes ensemble density of members equals the likelihood of a physical outcome
options.text: Correct, because members at the extremes of a spread carry correspondingly low odds

options.misconception: believes a single far-out member is necessarily a coding error
options.text: Correct, because a member that far outside the spread must be a numerical artefact

options.misconception: believes the ensemble spread is a hard physical limit the truth cannot cross
options.text: Partly wrong, because the spread is a physical error bar that the truth cannot leave

questions.explanation: The expected factor is 1.07 for 1.0 K of warming, and station A's 2.14 over 2.00 is exactly 1.07 while station B's 5.80 over 4.00 is 1.45, far more than a single kelvin can supply. The temptation is to read the larger change as more intense extreme rainfall, but a seven percent per kelvin rule cannot produce a forty-five percent rise, so B needs another process such as a change in storm structure or in the number of storms. The remaining two figures each break the comparison by subtracting instead of dividing, or by inverting the ratio.
questions.hint: Form a ratio for each station and compare it with 1.07 rather than comparing the changes.

options.misconception: inverts the ratio when checking a station against the scaling

answer.exemplar: Over the shared 90 years the ring-width index would be regressed against the measured temperature to recover a calibration curve, and the sign and strength of that fit would say how well this tree tracks temperature; the residuals matter as much as the correlation, because a tight fit that still trends, or one that only holds in the warm part of the overlap, indicates the response is not stationary. The overlap cannot remove the real limitation, which is the assumption that the tree's growth response was the same during the uncalibrated centuries: a century of changed soils, competitors, pests or management could shift the curve without leaving a trace in the overlap years, and no amount of extra overlap can test that because the uncalibrated period is by definition unobserved.

questions.explanation: A strong answer sets out the regression on the overlap, checks the residuals and the variance explained rather than quoting a correlation alone, and then names stationarity of the growth-to-climate response as the assumption the overlap cannot test. It should also note that lengthening the overlap does not help, because the extrapolation problem lies in unobserved biology rather than in sample size. An answer that treats a high correlation as proof, or that proposes more overlap as the fix, misplaces where the uncertainty lives.
questions.hint: Ask what the shared period can test, and what it structurally cannot test.
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a proxy calibration on its overlap and name its irreducible limitation

questions.explanation: A desert skin at midday is expected to run far above the 2 m air because the surface has no latent heat sink and the extra energy is stored in the top centimetre, so an on-site radiometer reading near 55 degrees confirms that the satellite is right. Measuring the same quantity the sensor measures is the only check that can separate physics from calibration; averaging the two numbers or adjusting the station to match destroys the comparison. Air records can only corroborate the air value, and assuming one instrument is correct in advance is the mistake the check exists to avoid.
questions.hint: Compare like with like: the satellite measures skin temperature, not air temperature.
questions.learningObjective: design a ground check that separates a real surface and air difference from an instrument bias

options.text: Measure the surface skin temperature on site with a calibrated hand radiometer

options.misconception: believes comparing with air records can measure a skin temperature
options.text: Compare the satellite value with nearby air records to build a regional bias

options.misconception: believes averaging two different quantities resolves the disagreement between them
options.text: Average the satellite and station values together to obtain a single temperature

options.misconception: assumes one of the two instruments must be right before any check is made
options.text: Recalibrate the ground weather station so that it matches the satellite reading

questions.explanation: Evaporation is the pathway the available energy takes when there is water at the surface, so as the soil dries the latent heat flux must fall, and the energy it no longer consumes appears as sensible heat heating the air. That swap is the first thing to move and it needs no change in the incoming radiation. Dry soil is darker than wet soil, so the net radiation arrow typically grows rather than shrinks, and canopy shading is not the control variable once the vegetation is still green and the water supply is what has changed.
questions.hint: One arrow is the plant's only way to spend energy; watch which one the water shortage removes.
questions.learningObjective: read a surface energy balance diagram and predict the first response to soil drying

options.text: Latent heat flux falls while sensible heat flux rises as dry soil limits evaporation

options.misconception: believes a drier surface is brighter and so loses energy to reflection
options.text: Net radiation falls because the drier surface reflects more sunlight back to space

options.misconception: believes the soil pulls heat downward out of the air as it dries
options.text: Ground heat flux rises as the air hands its warmth to the cooling surface below

options.misconception: believes canopy shading controls the energy split after drying
options.text: Shortwave absorption rises because the thinner canopy no longer shades the soil

questions.explanation: Atmospheric water of 12,900 cubic kilometres turning over at 496,000 cubic kilometres a year is replaced about 38 times a year, so the mean time in the atmosphere is 365 divided by 38, roughly 9.5 days. The residence time is the ratio of the inventory to the flux through the reservoir, which is why choosing the right turnover matters: using ocean evaporation alone or land precipitation alone gives a different number for a global storage. Reading the turnover count as a time in years is the unit slip that produces the largest of the wrong answers.
questions.hint: Divide the stored volume by the volume that passes through it in a year, then convert years to days.
questions.learningObjective: compute an atmospheric water residence time from inventory and flux

options.text: About 9.5 days, because storage divided by the turnover flux gives storage time

options.misconception: reports the turnover count per year as though it were the storage time
options.text: About 38 years, because the turnover count per year is read as a residence time

options.misconception: uses ocean evaporation alone and omits the land contribution to turnover
options.text: About 11 days, because ocean evaporation alone is used as the turnover flux

options.misconception: uses land precipitation alone as the flux for a global storage figure
options.text: About 42 days, because precipitation on land alone is used as the turnover flux

questions.explanation: Roof reflectance shows up as the heat island chiefly at night, so the test must compare like blocks on the same nights while holding albedo, storeys, tree cover and wind exposure comparable, which is what a matched pair with simultaneous sensors provides. Comparing a single roof, or the same roof on two different afternoons, leaves the night-time cooling, the local geometry and the weather free to explain the difference instead. Treating the whole city as treated removes the untreated comparison entirely, so any change in the weather or the traffic over the study period is absorbed into the result as if it were the coating.
questions.hint: The coating mainly works at night, so both measurements must share the same night and similar surroundings.
questions.learningObjective: design a field test that isolates an urban heat island intervention from confounders

options.text: Paired matched neighbourhoods, one coated and one bare, watched over the same nights

options.misconception: believes a single treated site still identifies the effect of the coating
options.text: One coated roof watched for a summer, with no untreated comparison roof nearby

options.misconception: confounds the coating with the weather on the day of each measurement
options.text: The same roof before and after coating, watched on two different afternoons

options.misconception: believes a before-and-after comparison is free of confounding over time
options.text: Every roof in the city coated, with the heat compared to a pre-coating archive

questions.explanation: Stakes spread across the accumulation, firn and ablation zones give the point balance, and repeat geodetic surveys of the whole surface give the glacier-wide number independently, so the two must agree for the programme to be trusted. That design controls the two dominant error sources, spatial sampling bias and measurement and conversion error, including the densification of the firn and melt that is hidden below the surface. A single stake samples one flow line, an outline image says nothing about the elevation change on the ice, and a webcam depth is snow height, which becomes mass only through a density that varies with settling and depth.
questions.hint: Combine a point method with an independent whole-ice measurement so each can check the other.
questions.learningObjective: design a glacier mass balance programme and name the error sources it controls

options.text: Annual stakes spread across the ice plus repeat geodetic surveys of the whole glacier

options.misconception: believes one stake on one flow line samples the whole glacier
options.text: A single stake at the snout, read once each year in late September after the melt

options.misconception: believes an outline change resolves the elevation change on the ice
options.text: Satellite images of the glacier outline each spring, with no field measurements at all

options.misconception: believes snow depth converts to mass with one universal fixed density
options.text: Snow depth read from a mountain webcam and converted to mass with one fixed density
